title: GINA 2019: a fundamental change in asthma management
authors: Reddel HK, FitzGerald JM, Bateman ED, Bacharier LB, Becker A, Brusselle G, et al.
funder: No support statement is given. The authors are members of the GINA Science Committee or the GINA Board; the article states that GINA does not accept donations and that its work is supported only by the sale and licensing of GINA reports and other publications and by the voluntary work of committee members.
authorConflicts: Most authors declare grants, advisory board fees, lecture fees or data monitoring committee fees from manufacturers of asthma medicines, among them AstraZeneca, GSK, Boehringer Ingelheim, Novartis, Teva and Sanofi, outside the submitted work.
result: In April 2019 the Global Initiative for Asthma stopped recommending treatment of asthma in adults and adolescents with short-acting beta2-agonists alone, recommending instead symptom-driven treatment in mild asthma or daily inhaled corticosteroid-containing treatment, to reduce the risk of serious exacerbations. The stated grounds include case-control studies linking overuse of short-acting agonists to asthma death, randomised trials finding no advantage of regular over as-needed use, the finding of the UK National Review of Asthma Deaths that 9% of asthma deaths occurred in patients treated with a short-acting agonist alone and 39% were associated with excess prescriptions for such agonists, and an almost two-thirds reduction in severe exacerbations with as-needed low-dose budesonide-formoterol compared with as-needed short-acting agonist. In the SYGMA 1 trial 12% of patients receiving as-needed short-acting agonist had a severe exacerbation within 12 months. Among adults with apparently mild asthma, 30-37% of those with acute asthma, 16% of those with near-fatal asthma and 15-20% of those dying of asthma had symptoms less than weekly in the previous three months.
